title: Intel Cuts IT Jobs as Tan's Cost Drive Extends Into Year-End
text:
Intel Cuts IT Jobs as Tan's Cost Drive Extends Into Year-End — BigGo Finance Ask AI News Markets Earnings Calls Calendar Watchlist Podcasts Influencers Earnings Calls Calendar Watchlist Podcasts Influencers More Ask AI News Watchlist Holdings Markets Earnings Calls Calendar Podcasts Influencers Intel Cuts IT Jobs as Tan's Cost Drive Extends Into Year-End
 Add preferred source Intel has cut jobs in its global IT organization, with the reductions reported to have begun November 16, though the company declined to say how many positions were affected or which teams were hit. A spokesperson said the chipmaker continually reviews staffing to align resources with priorities but did not confirm a new round. The move extends a restructuring under CEO Lip-Bu Tan, who took over last year and has pushed to cut expenses and management layers. Intel's workforce stood at 81,100 at the end of September, down from 85,100 at the end of 2025 and 88,400 a year earlier. The company filed nine California WARN notices covering 222 employees between July and October. Shares closed at $55.17 on November 17, and Nvidia cut its Intel stake by 25% in the third quarter. Key Elements 
 Intel Lip-Bu Tan Nvidia Mobileye David Zinsner Pat Gelsinger Folsom, California Santa Clara City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System Intel has trimmed staff inside its global information technology organization, the latest step in a cost-cutting campaign that Chief Executive Lip-Bu Tan has kept running into the closing months of 2026. The reductions were reported to have started November 16, though their size and geographic spread could not be established.
 Asked about the cuts, a company spokesperson declined to give a headcount or name the teams involved. "As part of our broader strategy to become a more focused and efficient company, we continually assess our workforce to ensure priorities and resources are appropriately aligned," the spokesperson said. The statement did not explicitly confirm a fresh round of layoffs.
 The cuts would follow a string of smaller reductions and organizational changes at the chipmaker this year. In July, Intel pared staff in its Data Center and AI Group. Between July and October, it filed nine separate Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification notices in California covering 222 employees in total. The most recent, dated October 22, covered 67 permanent layoffs at the company's Folsom campus with an effective date of October 31, while earlier filings in July and September covered reductions at Santa Clara facilities. No new WARN notice had surfaced as of November 17, though the absence of a filing does not rule out smaller or overseas cuts.
 Headcount has been falling steadily. Intel reported 81,100 employees as of September 26, including 76,500 at Intel itself and 4,600 at Mobileye and other subsidiaries, according to its third-quarter results. That compares with 85,100 at the end of 2025 and 88,400 a year earlier.
 Date Total workforce 
 Late September 2026 81,100 
 End of 2025 85,100 
 End of 2024 (one year earlier) 88,400 
 Note: Figures are from Intel's third-quarter financial results and company filings; the September 2026 total includes 4,600 employees at Mobileye and other subsidiaries.
 The current wave traces back to a plan announced in 2024 under then-CEO Pat Gelsinger to eliminate more than 15,000 positions, roughly 15% of the workforce. Tan, who took the top job last year, has said his own restructuring is meant to lower expenses, strip out management layers and move resources away from lower-priority programs.
 Investor sentiment has been strained. Intel shares closed at $55.17 on November 17 after a difficult stretch. A regulatory filing showed Nvidia (NVDA) cut its Intel stake by 25% in the third quarter, reducing its position to about 161.1 million shares from roughly 214.8 million.
 The company also faces a proposed shareholder class-action suit in federal court in San Jose. The case, led by Michigan's City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System, alleges that executives, including Tan and Chief Financial Officer David Zinsner, were slow to disclose how softening personal computer demand and excess inventory would hit results. The claims have not been proven.
 For investors, the IT reductions signal that operating expenses will keep falling even as Intel tries to rebuild its manufacturing position and win ground in AI chips, where it has lost share. The lack of disclosed numbers leaves analysts to infer the savings from payroll totals and the pace of WARN filings, and any acceleration in the fourth quarter would sharpen the focus on how much of the cost base Tan intends to remove before margins improve.
